But the fragmentary structure, with few scenes stretching to any substantial length, paradoxically creates a sense of dramatic inertia that the vibrant performances cannot overcome.
By trusting its audience to inhabit those uncertainties alongside Dre and Des, Lombe has created a poignant and deeply human drama that lingers long after the final scene.
Shifters may be a very small play but it strikes a symphony of resonant chords.
Shifters is a mosaic of meticulously cut and polished gems.

I felt the same about the couple in Shifters: this relationship ultimately tracks the failure of two people to be in the right place and time to be what and who the other needs, to heal each other’s traumas.

The two smart and witty characters are playful combatants and reluctant soulmates; Heather Agyepong and Daniel Ezra portray them with convincing rapport and an engaging repertoire of precise and revealing gestures and expressions.
Ms. Lombe’s one-act play offers glimmers of insight, along with some platitudes, and Ms. Linton and her players deliver them with grace and charm.
Shifters deserves celebration as a distinctly Black love story written with a clear depth of care, authenticity, humor, and thoughtful poetry by Congolese British playwright Benedict Lombe.
SHIFTERS at the Theatre is everything magical about live theater and the human imagination.
Agyepong and Ezra take these fully realized characters and give them a believable, natural rapport, helping Shifters transcend its familiar setup.
Shifters runs 45 minutes longer than Payne’s play, but it feels slighter and less substantial.
Shifters is not your typical play — the director and the playwright built something rare together.

cn.t: This intimate two-hander about love across time earns praise for its stellar leads and emotional resonance, though some critics find it derivative of similar British romances. The minimalist staging and non-linear structure mostly enchant.
